**Caças e aviões acrobáticos chegam a 9: **Fighters and aerobatic airplanes reach 9 G**, and an aircraft carrier catapult takes the airplane to more than **250 km/h in less than 2 seconds**. **Hiperventilar** é respirar além do nec: **Hyperventilating** is breathing more than necessary and blowing off too much **carbon dioxide**. Anxiety, pain, stress and altitude itself can trigger it. The dizziness and tingling resemble hypoxia, but the mechanism is different.
**Hipotermia** é a temperatura central d: **Hypothermia** is a core temperature of **35 °C or less**. At around **34 °C**, the brain already works more slowly. Shivering, the main defense, **decreases around 32 °C and stops near 30 °C**. Below that, the heart slows and the risk of **arrhythmia** soars.
**Hipóxia** é a falta de oxigênio nos te: **Hypoxia** is a lack of oxygen in the tissues, from insufficient supply or use. Altitude is only one of the causes: the failure can happen at any step between the air and the cell. That is why aerospace medicine divides it into **four mechanisms**, which can add up.
**Impacto** é uma aceleração de **fração: **Impact** is an acceleration lasting a **fraction of a second**: the jolt of a hard landing, of an accident or of leaving an ejection seat. It differs from the sustained G of turns, which lasts seconds (See M1V7). In an impact, blood has no time to shift; what suffers is the **structure of the body**: bones, ligaments and organs that keep moving when the seat has already stopped.
**Lei de Boyle:** com a temperatura cons: **Boyle's law:** at constant temperature, pressure and volume move in opposite directions (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂). Less pressure, more volume. That is why a sealed bag puffs up during the climb, and air trapped in the body's cavities does the same.
**Lei de Charles:** com a pressão consta: **Charles's law:** at constant pressure, volume follows absolute temperature; in a rigid container, it is the pressure that follows (**Gay-Lussac**). Because the body regulates its own temperature, the effect shows up in equipment: in the cold, the **oxygen cylinder** reads lower pressure without having lost any gas.
**Lei de Dalton:** a pressão total do ar: **Dalton's law:** the total pressure of air is the sum of the pressures of each gas. Oxygen is still 20.95% of dry air, but its **partial pressure** falls along with total pressure, and that is what pushes oxygen into the blood. Once humidified in the airways, inspired oxygen equals 0.2095 × (PB − 47): **149 mmHg at sea level, 108 mmHg at 8,000 ft and 70 mmHg at 18,000 ft**. This gives rise to **hypoxic hypoxia** and the need for supplemental oxygen.
**Lei de Henry:** a quantidade de gás di: **Henry's law:** the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid follows that gas's pressure. When pressure falls, tissues become **supersaturated with nitrogen**, which tends to come out as bubbles: this is the mechanism of **decompression sickness** (See M1V3). The risk grows with rapid decompressions and after diving with compressed gas.
**Pressurizar não dispensa o oxigênio.**: **Pressurization does not replace oxygen.** A failure or a decompression is always possible, which is why supplemental oxygen remains on board (See M1V3).

A **ICRP**, comissão internacional de pr: The **ICRP**, the international commission on radiological protection, recommends for exposed workers an effective dose of **20 mSv per year, averaged over 5 years**, without exceeding **50 mSv in any single year**; the **FAA** adopts the same values. For the general public, the limit is **1 mSv per year**. These numbers do not separate safe from dangerous: they are the **ceiling of the acceptable**. Medical exams do not count toward it. The limits serve two purposes: avoiding **tissue reactions**, which only appear above a threshold, and keeping the risk of **cancer**, which has no threshold, low. For the **lens of the eye**, the ICRP lowered the estimated **cataract** threshold to about **0.5 Gy** and the occupational eye limit from 150 to **20 mSv per year**, averaged over 5 years; flight doses are far below that.
A **atmosfera** é a camada de gases que: The **atmosphere** is the layer of gases surrounding the Earth. Dry air is **78.08% nitrogen**, **20.95% oxygen**, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus traces of other gases. Water vapor varies with the weather. Within the flight range, this recipe barely changes.
A **centrífuga humana** gira uma cabine: The **human centrifuge** spins a cabin on a long arm and creates **sustained G**, safely, with doctors monitoring the pilot by video and electrocardiogram. Under the **NATO** standard, training uses the aircraft's G, usually **up to 9 G**, with a rapid onset of at least **3 G per second**, and each person learns to recognize **their own signs** of impending G-LOC and to perform the right maneuver.
A **curva de dissociação da oxi-hemoglob: The **oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve** explains the danger: at first, saturation holds up; past a certain point, each further drop in pressure brings saturation down faster and faster. Altitude, exposure time, breathing and disease change this response. Finding out at which of the four steps oxygen failed is the first step to correcting it.
A **manobra anti-G** é ativa. O piloto *: The **anti-G straining maneuver** is active. The pilot **forcefully tenses the legs, abdomen and arms** and strains to exhale against a **closed glottis** for **3 to 4 seconds**, followed by a **quick inhalation**, repeating the cycle. Pressure in the chest rises and pushes blood toward the head. Well trained, it provided about **3 G** of protection; tensing alone, about **2 G**. It is tiring, and the FAA warns: **do not perform it at full strength at 1 G**, to avoid injury.
The **brace position** also protects. In **17 sled tests**, the FAA found that resting **the hands and head on the seatback in front** only helped if the seatback was locked; with a seatback that **breaks over** or **absorbs energy**, it made the head strike worse. With the **hands down, next to the legs**, the risk to the **head and neck** fell significantly for all seatbacks, and the FAA's official recommendation changed.
A **umidade relativa** mostra quanto do: **Relative humidity** shows how much of the vapor possible at that temperature is already in the air. Heated without gaining vapor, air becomes relatively drier. The **dew point** is the temperature at which air, as it cools, becomes saturated. The closer the temperature is to it, the closer the air is to saturation, which does not guarantee fog.
A **vibração de corpo inteiro** chega pe: **Whole-body vibration** arrives through the **seat**, the backrest and the floor, and is measured as **acceleration**, in **meters per second squared (m/s²)**. The body does not react equally to all frequencies. On the **vertical** axis, from feet to head, the greatest sensitivity is between **4 and 8 Hz**, the range of the body's main **resonance**, in which it amplifies the movement; on the lateral axis, between **1 and 2 Hz**.
A **visão noturna** é das mais sensíveis: **Night vision** is among the most sensitive and can worsen even at moderate altitudes. Then recent memory, reasoning and fine movements suffer. In chamber training, each person learns to recognize their own set of symptoms: the **individual hypoxia signature**.
A **água fria** é o cenário mais traiçoe: **Cold water** is the most treacherous setting, and the rule is **1-10-1**. In the **first minute**, **cold shock** causes gasping: the danger is **inhaling water**, so controlling breathing comes before anything else. Then there are about **10 minutes of useful movement** before the muscles fail. Hypothermia takes **at least half an hour** and, by about **1 hour**, leads to unconsciousness. **Most deaths happen at the start, not from hypothermia.**

The training is recommended for all pilots (See M3V3). The training also takes a toll on the body: in a study of **1,627 students**, **5.6%** had some adverse effect; the most common was **barotrauma of the ear and sinuses** (69% of these cases), followed by respiratory problems and **decompression sickness**.
